rv.q: When an audible gasp ripples across the audience at the mere snap of a pencil, it’s clear that their production has us right in the palm of its hand.
Here, they are a pair of theatrical pyrotechnicians who set Rebeck’s sometimes creaky play alight.

Instead this is an evening distinguished by its two lead performances: Pullman, painfully and defiantly nasty; Harbour superb as Michael — a gentle bear of a man haunted by his own fragilities and ill-suited to a tough, grasping world.
With its pacey first half and the acting of Henry and the two male leads, Mad House holds your attention.
This bad-ish taste comedy from US playwright Theresa Rebeck stumbles between misanthropic yucks and a desire to say something more sensitive and profound about the human condition.
It’s still a thought-provoking piece, but you’re left wondering what might have been.
It is ultimately a play with bits of brilliance, aspiring for the power and reach of an Arthur Miller or Eugene O’Neill drama but falling – heroically – short.
The dark comedy draws you in, but hits the snag of leaving you a bit high and dry when you yourself are required to care.
It’s an entertaining but uninspired showcase for two megawatt US talents...
Though it’s loaded with crisp dialogue and moments of wince-inducing viciousness, Rebeck’s script suffers from its low stakes and ponderous pace.
Once you’ve watched Mad House, you won’t want to erase this play from memory.
Mad House perfectly captures the imperfect, complex family dynamic.
This is writing that feels engrossing in the moment, but less significant once that moment has passed, and Moritz von Stuelpnagel’s direction is correspondingly polished.
The trouble is that the two plays never quite gel into one satisfying whole.
Despite the light touch of the hard-working cast, the play’s over-inflated highs and lows are like eating a meal of sugary food: It provides a rush, but leaves you unsatisfied.
Theresa Rebeck's Mad House is theatrical brilliance, a story we can all identify with, but beautifully told and elevated by complex characters.
Mad House is a truly wonderful piece of theatre that plays on your mind long after you leave the theatre.

cn.t: Rebeck's dysfunctional family drama delivers powerhouse performances from Pullman and Harbour, but critics are divided on whether the dark comedy's tonal shifts work, with some finding it cathartic and others seeing it as directionless.
